newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya groups plan more protests after bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Kenya groups plan more protests after bloodshed.

text.p: Opposition-backed groups calling for constitutional reforms before this year's general election vowed on Tuesday to step up their campaign of public protest a day after the most violent clashes with police for seven years.

But Kenyan officials and police said they expected the calls for more protests largely to go unheeded and Kenya's capital and towns were reported calm and back to business after closing down on Monday.

Security remained tight in Nairobi for a summit of regional presidents on war in Sudan. Riot police waited in the rain near the hotels where foreign leaders were staying and patrolled shopping centres around Nairobi wielding pick-axe handles.

Opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies in the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) ordered a new demonstration on Wednesday to put pressure on the government and bring conflict in Kenya to the attention of visiting leaders.
But Kenyan officials ridiculed the NCEC's ability to disrupt the six-nation summit at State House in Nairobi which opened on Tuesday and ends on Wednesday morning hosted by President Daniel arap Moi.
"What can they achieve? I don't see anyone demonstrating here," said a senior official at heavily-guarded State House.
Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since unrest in 1991 that helped push Moi to allow multi-party elections.
The NCEC called for three days of national mourning from Wednesday to Friday "for the gallant sons and daughters who were killed by the government during the "Saba Saba" commemoration.

But on the bustling streets of Nairobi it was unclear who was observing the call for mourning and Nairobi University students, the bedrock of the opposition-backed rallies, were busy with examinations.

"There is a determination of and a capacity by Kenyans to ensure that no election is held before reform is effected," the NCEC said. "The cry that there be no elections before reform is the cry of every Kenyan."

The NCEC said it was planning a national strike and holding protests outside provincial administration centres as part of its non-violent campaign to force constitutional changes, which Moi says cannot be introduced before the general election.
No date has been set for the parliamentary and presidential polls in which Moi, 73, is still widely expected to win another five-year term because of squabbling among opposition leaders.

"I don't think that Kenyans will heed that call. What Kenyans are saying is that all avenues open for change have not been exploited. Why should people turn to violence," said police spokesman Assistant Commissioner Peter Kimanthi in Nairobi.

He said four people died in the Rift Valley town of Nyahururu on Monday, four died in Nairobi and one in Thika. Police beat demonstrators and were locked in running battles for hours with stone-throwing students at several locations.

Kenyan newspapers splashed the bloodshed of Monday on their front pages. The East African Standard trumpeted what it said was a "National day of shame and disgrace" and said the losers were innocent Kenyans.
But in an editorial it said violence would never bring results and the tension was scaring away foreign investors.
The independent Daily Nation said the government must "defuse this ticking bomb" of unrest and heed calls for reform.

"The country cannot sustain this state of affairs for long. The plain truth is that if the protagonists continue with this dangerous game of open belligerence, we may not have much of a country to talk about," the newspaper said in an editorial.
Economic analysts said the acid test in the run-up to the polls would be whether political tension was reined in and fast evaporating investor confidence returned because of stability.
The Nairobi stock exchange index edged up 17.46 points on Monday but traded volume fell to the year's low at 5.1 billion shillings on 140,382 shares after most traders went home early.
